title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F03
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 48 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

There are some small blue patches scattered across the image, which could be areas of open water or meltwater ponds. The glacier's terminus is visible, and the image provides a good overview of the glacier's extent and the surrounding environment. The image can be used to monitor the glacier's response to climate change, as well as to study the glacier's dynamics and the processes that govern its behavior. The image also provides a valuable resource for researchers and policymakers who are interested in understanding the impacts of climate change on the cryosphere and the broader Earth system.

The following MOOC lectures explain SAR principles and its application for detecting ground surface deformation and subsidence:

SAR Principles
• ESA Echoes in Space - History: The SAR principle: This lecture covers the fundamentals of "Aperture Synthesis," explaining how SAR emulates a large antenna by taking multiple measurements during satellite motion. It also discusses "Doppler beam sharpening," which utilizes the Doppler shift of returning echoes to achieve high spatial resolution in the azimuth direction.

Ground Surface Deformation and Subsidence
• ESA Echoes in Space - Hazard: Introduction to Subsidence Monitoring: This lecture explains that deformation is measured by analyzing the phase of the radar wave. By comparing the phase difference when a satellite returns to the same location, movements of millimetres or centimetres can be mapped. It specifically addresses subsidence, earthquakes, and volcanic activity, and introduces "permanent scatterer interferometry" for long-term monitoring of movements as small as a few millimetres per year.
• ESA Echoes in Space - Hazard: Saving lives when disaster strikes: This lecture focuses on "repeat-pass SAR interferometry," which detects phase differences between pre- and post-event data to derive large-scale topographic displacements (such as landslides and earthquake-induced deformations) with millimetric precision.

Here are the relevant MOOC lecture excerpts explaining synthetic aperture radar (SAR) principles and its application in detecting ground surface deformation and subsidence:

1. ESA Echoes in Space - History: The SAR Principle
Key Concepts:
• Challenges of Imaging Radar: Radar wavelengths (centimetres to metres) are much larger than optical wavelengths, requiring proportionally larger systems for similar detail.
• Oblique Viewing: SAR systems look sideways rather than straight down to use timing delays for distance measurement, compensating for poor directional resolution.
• Aperture Synthesis: To achieve high azimuth resolution (e.g., 30 metres), SAR uses multiple small antennas or a single antenna moved incrementally to simulate a much larger antenna (e.g., synthesising a 1 km antenna with a 10 m antenna).
• Doppler Beam Sharpening: Exploits the Doppler shift of returning signals to narrow the effective beam width. As a target moves through the beam, its relative motion changes the frequency of the returned signal, allowing precise location determination within the beam.

2. ESA Echoes in Space - Hazard: Introduction to Subsidence Monitoring
Key Concepts:
• Phase Measurement in Radar Interferometry: SAR measures the phase of the returned wave. If the ground surface shifts between measurements, the extra distance travelled by the wave (a fraction of the wavelength) changes the phase, allowing detection of movement.
• Sensitivity to Small Movements: At C-band (wavelength ~5 cm), SAR can detect ground movements as small as centimetres or even millimetres. Larger shifts (multiple wavelengths) are harder to measure.
• Subsidence and Deformation Monitoring: SAR can track slow surface changes (e.g., subsidence, volcanic activity) over time. Techniques like Permanent Scatterer Interferometry (PSI) focus on stable targets to measure movements as small as a few millimetres per year.
• Limitations: The method works best for small, gradual movements. Rapid or large shifts can exceed the measurable phase change.

Summary of Applications
• Ground Deformation Detection: SAR’s phase sensitivity allows it to measure subtle ground movements caused by subsidence, earthquakes, or volcanic activity.
• Long-Term Monitoring: By analysing phase changes over time, SAR can track slow surface deformations with high precision.

items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for narratives about wildfires, then find a MOOC lecture that teaches the satellite techniques used to detect and monitor active fires from space.

answers.text:
Here are the results for your request:

EO Dashboard Narratives on Wildfires
1. Australian bushfires in 2019-2020 (https://ESA-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-narratives/australian-bushfires.md)
   • Theme: Atmosphere
   • Key Focus: Use of Copernicus Sentinel-5P (Tropomi instrument) to monitor wildfire emissions (CO, CO₂, NO₂).
   • Techniques: Satellite-based detection of atmospheric pollutants to analyze fire intensity and environmental impact.

2. STAC Collections for Fire Monitoring
   • EPA_Forest_fire_Methane_Daily (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/EPA_Forest_fire_Methane_Daily/collection.json)
     • Data: Daily methane emissions from forest fires (United States).
   • EPA_Forest_fire_Methane_Yearly (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/EPA_Forest_fire_Methane_Yearly/collection.json)
     • Data: Yearly methane emissions from forest fires.

MOOC Lecture on Satellite Techniques for Fire Monitoring
Fire Monitoring: Fire monitoring with Remote Sensing (https://example.com/mooc-fire-monitoring)
• Learning Goals:
  • Understand how remote sensing supports fire monitoring.
  • Distinguish between fire intensity (during the fire) and fire severity (post-fire burn severity).
  • Monitor emissions, smoke, fire size, direction, and post-fire vegetation recovery.
• Key Techniques:
  • Active Fire Detection: Monitoring smoke, temperature, and fire size/direction.
  • Burn Severity Monitoring: Using the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) with near-infrared and shortwave infrared bands.
  • Spectral Response: Analyzing vegetation and soil signatures to assess burn severity.

The EO Dashboard contains a narrative on the Australian bushfires of 2019-2020, which demonstrates the use of the TROPOMI instrument on Sentinel-5P to monitor carbon monoxide (CO) levels as a proxy for estimating CO2 emissions from wildfires.

Regarding educational materials, the MOOC lecture "Fire Monitoring: Fire monitoring with Remote Sensing" covers the following techniques:
• Active Fire Detection: Using platforms like FIRMS (NASA MODIS, NASA VIIRS, NOAA Suomi NPP) and EFIS, which utilize mid-infrared radiation emissions and cloud mass testing to detect active fires.
• Burn Severity Monitoring: Using the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR), which compares pre- and post-fire imagery using near-infrared and shortwave infrared bands to assess vegetation damage.

Here is what I found:

EO Dashboard Narratives on Wildfires
The EO Dashboard narrative about wildfires discusses the 2019-2020 Australian bushfires, emphasizing their significant environmental impact, including the emission of 700 million metric tons of CO2. It highlights the role of satellite data, particularly from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P mission's TROPOMI instrument, in accurately measuring emissions and understanding the connection between wildfires and climate change.

MOOC Lecture on Satellite Techniques for Detecting and Monitoring Active Fires
Here are the relevant MOOC lecture chunks that teach satellite techniques for detecting and monitoring active fires from space:

[1] Fire Monitoring: Fire monitoring with Remote Sensing
Source: Fire Monitoring - Introduction

Content:
• Learning Goals:
  • Understand how remote sensing supports fire monitoring.
  • Distinguish between fire intensity (during a fire) and fire severity (after a fire).
  • Learn how to monitor fire burn severity using remote sensing data.

• Key Concepts:
  • Fire Triangle: Oxygen, heat, and fuel are essential for a fire to exist.
  • Fire Intensity: Energy released during a fire (e.g., temperature, duration, radiation power).
  • Fire Severity: Post-fire assessment of organic matter loss (above and below ground).

• Role of Earth Observation:
  • Prevention: Monitor hazard conditions (e.g., high temperatures, dry vegetation) and map risk areas.
  • Active Fires: Detect emissions (smoke), measure temperatures, and track fire size and direction.
  • Post-Fire: Monitor burned vegetation, soil, and vegetation recovery.

• Remote Sensing Techniques:
  • Spectral Response: Vegetation reflects differently in the near-infrared (NIR) and shortwave infrared (SWIR) bands compared to burned areas.
  • Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR): Uses NIR and SWIR bands to assess burn severity (high/medium/low severity).

items.question: Look up what the ESA Science Strategy says about monitoring forests and deforestation from space, then find a matching MOOC lecture on the same topic.

answers.text:
Here is what the ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy says about monitoring forests and deforestation from space, along with a matching MOOC lecture on the same topic:

ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy: Forests and Deforestation Monitoring
The ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy highlights the critical role of satellite-based monitoring in addressing Science Questions (SQs) related to forests and deforestation, including:

1. Global Carbon Cycle (SQ-01)
   • Forests act as key carbon sinks, and deforestation significantly impacts carbon cycles.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Quantify CO₂ and CH₄ emissions and removals.
     • Distinguish anthropogenic vs. natural emissions.
     • Quantify fluxes from managed lands.
   • Tipping Points: Directly linked to TP-05 (Tropical Forests), TP-06 (Boreal Forests), and TP-07 (Temperate Forests).

2. Land Biosphere Responses (SQ-02)
   • Focuses on how the land biosphere responds to human activity and climate change.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Quantify land source/sink distribution and drivers.
     • Quantify roles of climate and disturbances on the land carbon sink.
     • Quantify above-ground biomass in forests.
     • Catalogue climate impacts on crop health and forest mortality.

3. State of Land Ecosystems (SQ-55)
   • Improves ecosystem characterization by structure, composition, and functions worldwide.

4. Ecosystems Transitions (SQ-56)
   • Investigates where and how ecosystems are undergoing critical transitions.

Strategic Objectives Supporting Forest Monitoring
• SO-02: Advance Earth science understanding within key themes, including Ecosystem Health (ST-IV).
• SO-05: Maximize mission exploitation (2026–2031) to advance forest monitoring.
• SO-10: Foster collaboration through ESA Science Clusters and the Earth System Science Hub.
• SO-14: Promote open science and digital innovation, including AI/ML for analyzing EO data related to forests.

Key Missions and Data Sources
• Landsat: Optical and thermal data for vegetation dynamics.
• Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2: SAR and optical data for forest structure and composition.
• Radar Sensors: C-band (e.g., Sentinel-1) and L-band (e.g., future missions) for biomass and deforestation monitoring.

Matching MOOC Lecture
[1] ESA Echoes in Space - Land: Introduction to Forest Monitoring
This lecture covers:
• The role of radar sensors (C-band and L-band) in monitoring forests and deforestation.
• How radar can measure forest biomass, canopy height, and subtle changes like degradation or regrowth.

3. Tipping Points (TPs): Focus on tropical, boreal, and temperate forests (e.g., dieback, biomass changes).
